topics.title: Tropical storms
topics.intro: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same thing in different oceans: giant spinning storms fed by warm seas. Poseidon got the blame for storms at sea; today satellites track them days in advance.
topics.teach: Explain the conditions a tropical storm needs to form.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why tropical storms never form right on the Equator.
topics.hook: Same storm, different names: hurricane (Atlantic), typhoon (north-west Pacific), cyclone (Indian Ocean and South Pacific).

topics.title: Extreme weather in the UK
topics.intro: The UK’s weather is usually mild, but it has extremes: snow from Siberia, droughts, named storms and record heat. Each one tests how ready we are.
topics.teach: Explain what caused the “Beast from the East” in 2018.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which UK storm names {she} remembers, and how they are chosen.
topics.hook: Weather warnings are traffic lights: yellow be aware, amber be prepared, red take action.

topics.title: The UK’s physical landscapes
topics.intro: Under every British landscape is its rock. Hard, old rocks make the uplands of the north and west; younger, softer rocks make the lowlands of the south and east.
topics.teach: Explain the Tees–Exe line and what it divides.
topics.talk: Next time you are on a walk, ask {him} what rock might be underneath and how {she} could tell.
topics.hook: Old, hard rocks in the north and west make the uplands; younger, softer rocks in the south and east make the lowlands.

topics.title: Soils and farming
topics.intro: Farming depends on soil, climate and relief. That is why eastern England grows wheat and the wet hills of the west raise sheep.
topics.teach: Explain why arable farming is common in East Anglia.
topics.talk: Look at where the food in your fridge comes from and ask {him} about food miles.
topics.hook: Dry and flat in the east: crops. Wet and hilly in the west: sheep.

topics.title: Water and food security
topics.intro: Water and food are unevenly shared. Rivers that cross borders, like the Nile and the Euphrates, can bring countries together or push them apart.
topics.teach: Explain what “virtual water” means, with an example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how much water {she} thinks is used to make one burger.
topics.hook: Rivers ignore borders: whoever is upstream holds the tap.

topics.title: Tourism and its impacts
topics.intro: Tourism is one of the world’s biggest industries. It brings jobs and money, but too many visitors can damage the very places they come to see, from Venice to the Acropolis.
topics.teach: Explain the stages of Butler’s tourism life cycle.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether {she} thinks famous places should limit visitors.
topics.hook: Tourism can love a place to death: the trick is sharing the benefits without wrecking the place.

topics.title: Deserts and desertification
topics.intro: Deserts are defined by dryness, not heat: Antarctica is the biggest of all. On the edges of the Sahara, the Sahel shows how land can slowly turn to desert, and how people are fighting back.
topics.teach: Explain three causes of desertification in the Sahel.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why the Great Green Wall is being planted.
topics.hook: A desert is defined by dryness, not heat: under 250 mm of rain a year.

topics.title: The polar regions
topics.intro: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land; Antarctica is a continent surrounded by ocean. Both are warming fast, and what happens there affects everyone.
topics.teach: Explain how Antarctica is protected by international agreement.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why melting Arctic sea ice does not raise sea levels much but melting Antarctic ice does.
topics.hook: Arctic: an ocean ringed by land, with polar bears. Antarctica: land ringed by ocean, with penguins.

topics.title: Oceans under pressure
topics.intro: Oceans cover about 71% of the Earth. They feed billions, steady the climate and hold most of its life, but plastic, overfishing and warming are taking their toll.
topics.teach: Explain how plastic ends up in the middle of the Pacific.
topics.talk: Count the single-use plastics in your bin this week with {him}.
topics.hook: With about 71% of its surface under the sea, Earth could be called Planet Ocean.

topics.title: Africa: a continent of 54 countries
topics.intro: Africa is not a country. It has 54 of them, well over a thousand languages, the world’s youngest population and some of its fastest-growing cities and tech industries.
topics.teach: Explain two common stereotypes about Africa and why they are misleading.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to name five African countries and one fact about each.
topics.hook: Africa is a continent of 54 countries, not one country.

topics.title: Nigeria in depth
topics.intro: Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country and one of its biggest economies. Oil, film, farming and the megacity of Lagos make it a classic GCSE case study of a newly emerging economy.
topics.teach: Explain the advantages and problems oil has brought to Nigeria.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what Nollywood is.
topics.hook: Nigeria is named after the River Niger; Lagos is its megacity, Abuja its capital.

topics.title: China’s rise
topics.intro: In forty years China went from a mostly rural country to the world’s workshop. Its choices on population, energy and cities affect the whole planet.
topics.teach: Explain one benefit and one problem of the Three Gorges Dam.
topics.talk: Look at how many things in your house were made in China and ask {him} why.
topics.hook: In about forty years China went from a land of farms to “the workshop of the world”.

topics.title: India: monsoon, rivers and change
topics.intro: India is now the world’s most populous country. Its farming depends on the monsoon, its rivers are sacred, and its cities are hubs of the global economy.
topics.teach: Explain why the monsoon matters so much to India.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what causes the monsoon.
topics.hook: India’s year turns on the monsoon: months of dry weather, then the rain that feeds the country.

topics.title: Brazil and the Amazon
topics.intro: Brazil holds most of the Amazon, the largest rainforest on Earth. Who gets to decide its future: farmers, miners, indigenous peoples, the government, or the world?
topics.teach: Explain why the Amazon matters beyond Brazil.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether {she} thinks other countries should pay Brazil to protect the rainforest.
topics.hook: Brazil holds about 60% of the Amazon: what Brazil decides, the whole planet feels.

topics.title: Europe, the EU and borders
topics.intro: Borders are drawn by people. The European Union removed many of them for trade and travel; Brexit put some back. Borders shape trade, migration and identity.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the EU, the euro area and the Schengen area.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what changed for travellers after the UK left the EU.
topics.hook: Three different clubs: the EU (27 members), the euro (shared money) and Schengen (no routine passport checks).

topics.title: UK cities and regeneration
topics.intro: When old industries closed, whole districts of British cities emptied. Regeneration brings them back to life, but who benefits?
topics.teach: Explain the difference between brownfield and greenfield sites.
topics.talk: Ask {him} about a part of your nearest city that has been rebuilt.
topics.hook: Brownfield is brown like old bricks (built on before); greenfield is green like grass (never built on).

topics.title: Fieldwork, enquiry and GIS
topics.intro: Geographers go out and measure. Good fieldwork starts with a question, uses fair sampling and ends by asking how reliable the results are. GIS layers data on maps to reveal patterns.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between random, systematic and stratified sampling.
topics.talk: Plan a mini fieldwork question with {him}: is our street busier at 8 am or 11 am?
topics.hook: Ask, collect, present, analyse, conclude, then evaluate: examiners love that last step.

topics.title: Sustainability and the global goals
topics.intro: Sustainable development meets today’s needs without stealing from the future. In 2015 every UN member agreed 17 Sustainable Development Goals for 2030.
topics.teach: Explain what sustainable development means, using an example.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which of the 17 global goals {she} thinks matters most.
topics.hook: Meet today’s needs without stealing from tomorrow’s.

topics.title: World places: more countries and capitals
topics.intro: Twenty-six more countries to find, from Argentina to New Zealand, and their capitals. Several capitals are not the biggest city: Canberra, Ottawa, Brasília and Pretoria were chosen or built on purpose.
topics.teach: Name three capitals that are not their country’s largest city.
topics.talk: Quiz each other on capitals during a car journey.
topics.hook: Capitals are not always the biggest city: Canberra, Ottawa, Brasília and Pretoria were chosen on purpose.

topics.title: Making decisions: issue evaluation (GCSE taster)
topics.intro: GCSE geography ends with an issue to judge: a new dam, a coastal defence, a tourist resort. You weigh stakeholders, costs, benefits and sustainability, then make and defend a decision.
topics.teach: Explain how to structure a decision-making answer.
topics.talk: Pick a local issue (a new housing estate, a bypass) and ask {him} who would be for and against it.
topics.hook: Options, stakeholders, costs and benefits, a choice, a justification: then say why you rejected the rest.

topics.title: Inside the city: urban models (GCSE taster)
topics.intro: Cities are not random. Models like Burgess’s rings show how land use, building age and wealth change as you travel out from the centre.
topics.teach: Explain the zones of the Burgess model.
topics.talk: On a drive into town, ask {him} to spot when you move from suburbs to inner city to the CBD.
topics.hook: Burgess is a dartboard with the CBD as the bullseye; Hoyt slices the city like a pizza along its transport routes.

topics.title: Resources and conflict (GCSE taster)
topics.intro: When resources are scarce or newly reachable, countries compete for them: shared rivers, Arctic seabed, rare metals for phones. Geography helps explain where tensions arise.
topics.teach: Explain why the Arctic is becoming more contested.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which resources {her} phone needs, and where they might come from.
topics.hook: Scarce or shared resources breed tension: rivers, the Arctic seabed and the metals in your phone.

items.prompt: Which set of conditions does a tropical storm need to form?

options.text: Sea water above about 27 °C, away from the Equator
Cold water and strong winds blowing from the poles
options.feedback: They are fed by warm water: heat and moisture are their fuel.

options.text: Any stretch of sea, as long as it is windy
options.feedback: They need very warm water and the spin from the Earth’s rotation.

options.text: Warm land with high mountains nearby
options.feedback: They form over the ocean and weaken over land.

items.explain: Warm water evaporates into rising air; the Coriolis effect, from the Earth’s spin, sets the storm turning.
items.hook: Storm recipe: sea above about 27 °C, warm moist air rising, and the Earth’s spin to set it turning.
items.example: The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November, when the ocean is warmest.

items.prompt: Why do tropical storms not form right on the Equator?

options.text: The Earth’s spin is too weak there to turn them
The sea there is too cold for them to form
options.feedback: The water at the Equator is very warm.

options.text: There is almost no wind at the Equator
options.feedback: There is wind; the problem is the lack of spin.

options.text: They do form there, many times each year
options.feedback: They almost never form within about 5° of the Equator.

items.explain: The Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator and grows towards the poles.
items.hook: No spin at 0°: the Coriolis effect is zero on the Equator, so storms need about 5° of latitude to start turning.

items.prompt: In the north-west Pacific, near Japan and the Philippines, a tropical storm is called a…
items.explain: Hurricane (Atlantic and north-east Pacific), typhoon (north-west Pacific), cyclone (Indian Ocean and South Pacific). Same storm, different names.
items.hook: Typhoon for Tokyo (north-west Pacific); hurricane for the Atlantic; cyclone for the Indian Ocean.

items.prompt: What is the eye of a tropical storm like?

options.text: Calm, with light winds
The windiest part of the storm
options.feedback: The strongest winds are in the eyewall around it.

options.text: Full of heavy hail
options.feedback: The eye is calm, as sinking air clears the cloud.

options.text: Much colder than the rest
options.feedback: It is not especially cold.

items.explain: People caught in the eye sometimes think the storm is over, then the other side of the eyewall arrives.
items.hook: The eye is the calm at the centre: the eyewall whirling round it is the most violent part.

items.prompt: Which scale rates hurricanes from category 1 to 5 by wind speed?
items.explain: Category 5 means sustained winds over about 250 km/h. (The Beaufort scale is for ordinary winds; Richter and Mercalli are for earthquakes.)
items.hook: Saffir–Simpson for Storms, Richter for Rocking ground, Beaufort for Breezes.

items.prompt: Typhoon Haiyan hit the Philippines in 2013 and killed more than 6,000 people. What caused most of the deaths?

options.text: A storm surge flooding low coasts
Hailstones the size of tennis balls
options.feedback: Hail is rare in tropical storms.

options.text: Lightning strikes on crowded towns
options.feedback: Lightning was not the main killer.

options.text: Landslides on volcanic slopes
options.feedback: Landslides happened, but the surge killed far more.

items.explain: Low pressure and fierce winds raise the sea by several metres, flooding coastal towns.
items.hook: Low pressure lets the sea bulge up; fierce winds then shove that bulge onto the coast.
items.example: In 1953 a North Sea storm surge flooded the east coast of England, killing over 300 people.

items.prompt: Hurricane Katrina (2005) flooded about 80% of New Orleans. Why was a rich country hit so hard?

options.text: Its levees failed
The USA had no warning at all
options.feedback: Forecasters warned days in advance.

options.text: It was the strongest hurricane ever
options.feedback: It was category 3 at landfall.

options.text: Nobody had been told to leave
options.feedback: A mandatory evacuation was ordered, but many could not leave.

items.explain: About 1,800 people died. Poorer residents without cars found it hardest to evacuate.
items.hook: Katrina shows wealth is not enough: when the levees broke, the poorest were hit hardest.

items.prompt: Why do tropical storms weaken when they move over land?

options.text: They lose their warm, moist air
The land’s magnetism pulls them apart
options.feedback: Magnetism has nothing to do with it.

options.text: Trees absorb the wind
options.feedback: Friction helps, but the main reason is losing their fuel.

options.text: They gain strength from hills
options.feedback: They weaken quickly, though their rain can still cause floods far inland.

items.explain: Their fuel is warm water. Over land they run out of it.
items.hook: Take away the warm sea and the storm starves: no fuel, no fire.

items.prompt: Explain why the effects of a tropical storm can be greater in a poorer country than in a richer one. Use examples.
hints: A clear point about wealth and preparation
Warnings, evacuation and building quality
An example from a poorer country (e.g. Haiyan, Philippines 2013)
An example from a richer country, including any exceptions (e.g. Katrina, 2005)
A short conclusion
items.model: Poorer countries usually suffer more deaths because they have less money to prepare and respond. Warning systems may not reach everyone, and many people live in lightweight homes on low coasts, so a storm surge can sweep them away. When Typhoon Haiyan hit the Philippines in 2013, the surge flooded Tacloban and more than 6,000 people died. Richer countries can afford satellites, strong buildings, evacuation plans and emergency services, so deaths are usually lower, although damage costs are higher because property is worth more. However, wealth does not guarantee safety: Hurricane Katrina killed about 1,800 people in New Orleans in 2005 because the levees failed and poorer residents could not evacuate. So wealth reduces risk, but only if it is used to protect everyone.
items.passage:
Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines, November 2013: storm surge of several metres at Tacloban; more than 6,000 deaths; about 4 million people displaced.
Hurricane Katrina, USA, August 2005: category 3 at landfall; levees failed and about 80% of New Orleans flooded; about 1,800 deaths; damage over $100 billion.

items.prompt: What caused the “Beast from the East” in February and March 2018?

options.text: Freezing easterly winds from Siberia
Ash from a volcanic eruption in Iceland
options.feedback: No eruption was involved.

options.text: A tropical storm that drifted north
options.feedback: It was extreme cold, not a tropical storm.

options.text: The Gulf Stream stopping for a month
options.feedback: The North Atlantic Drift did not stop.

items.explain: Usually our weather comes from the mild Atlantic. When the wind swings round to the east in winter, it brings continental cold. Storm Emma added heavy snow.
items.hook: Beast from the East: a winter wind from the east brings Siberian cold instead of mild Atlantic air.

items.prompt: Why have UK storms been given names since 2015?

options.text: So people take warnings seriously
To honour famous British scientists
options.feedback: Names are chosen from public suggestions, not to honour anyone.

options.text: Because they are all hurricanes
options.feedback: Ordinary deep depressions are named when they are likely to cause severe impacts.

options.text: It is a tradition from Roman times
options.feedback: It started in 2015.

items.explain: The Met Office and Met Éireann (and now the Dutch weather service) name storms likely to bring amber or red warnings.
items.hook: UK storm names go A to Z, alternating male and female, but skip Q, U, X, Y and Z.
items.example: Storm Eunice, in February 2022, brought a record English gust of 122 mph at the Needles on the Isle of Wight.

items.prompt: The UK’s lowest recorded temperature, −27.2 °C, was measured in which country of the UK?
items.explain: It has been reached three times in the Scottish Highlands: at Braemar (1895 and 1982) and Altnaharra (1995).
items.hook: Height plus distance from the warm sea makes the Scottish Highlands the UK’s freezer.
items.example: Braemar, in the Cairngorms, has hit −27.2 °C twice, in 1895 and 1982.

items.prompt: Which of these is a typical response to drought in the UK?

options.text: A hosepipe ban
Cloud seeding over every city
options.feedback: The UK does not routinely seed clouds.

options.text: Closing schools to save water
options.feedback: Drought does not close schools.

options.text: Building new sea walls
options.feedback: Sea walls protect against coastal flooding, not drought.

items.explain: The long, hot summer of 1976 brought standpipes in streets; 2022 brought hosepipe bans across much of England.
items.hook: Drought responses grow step by step: save water, then a hosepipe ban, then standpipes in the street.
items.example: In the drought of 1976, the government even appointed a Minister for Drought.

items.prompt: Why might extreme rainfall in the UK become more common as the climate warms?

options.text: Warmer air holds more water vapour
Warmer air holds less water vapour
options.feedback: It is the opposite: about 7% more water vapour per °C.

options.text: The UK is drifting towards the Equator
options.feedback: Plates move only a few centimetres a year.

options.text: Rainfall will not change at all
options.feedback: Scientists expect wetter winters and more intense downpours.

items.explain: This is why wetter winters and more intense summer storms are both expected.
items.hook: Every 1 °C warmer, air holds about 7% more water vapour: a bigger sponge to wring out.
items.example: Storm Desmond, in December 2015, dropped a UK record 341 mm of rain in 24 hours at Honister Pass in Cumbria.

items.prompt: What does a Met Office RED weather warning mean?

options.text: Dangerous weather: take action now
Be aware of minor disruption
options.feedback: That is yellow.

options.text: Be prepared for travel delays
options.feedback: That is amber.

options.text: Very hot sun: wear sun cream
options.feedback: Heat can bring warnings too, but red means danger to life.

items.explain: Yellow, amber, red: from “be aware” to “take action”.
items.hook: Traffic lights for weather: yellow be aware, amber be prepared, red take action.
items.example: In July 2022 the Met Office issued its first ever red warning for extreme heat.

items.prompt: Explain how one extreme weather event affected people in the UK and how they responded.
hints: Name the event and when it happened
What caused it (briefly)
At least two effects on people (travel, schools, health, economy)
How people and authorities responded
A judgement on how well the UK coped
items.model: The “Beast from the East” in late February and early March 2018 brought bitterly cold easterly winds from Siberia, and when it met Storm Emma heavy snow fell across much of the UK. Roads and railways closed, thousands of schools shut, and some drivers were stranded overnight on motorways. Supermarkets ran short of bread and milk, and burst pipes left homes without water when the thaw came. The Met Office issued rare red warnings, councils gritted main roads and the army helped to rescue stranded people. The UK coped reasonably well with warnings and emergency help, but the disruption showed that a country used to mild winters is not well equipped for heavy snow.
items.passage: The “Beast from the East”, late February to early March 2018: easterly winds from Siberia, then Storm Emma from the south. Heavy snow and temperatures below −10 °C in places. Red weather warnings issued; schools, roads and railways closed; the army helped stranded drivers.

items.prompt: What does the Tees–Exe line roughly divide?

options.text: Upland from lowland Britain
England from Scotland
options.feedback: It runs from the River Tees in the north-east to the River Exe in Devon.

options.text: Wet farmland from dry farmland
options.feedback: Rainfall differs too, but the line is mainly about rock and height.

options.text: Cities from the countryside
options.feedback: Both sides have cities and countryside.

items.explain: Draw a line from the mouth of the Tees to the mouth of the Exe: hills and mountains mostly lie to the north-west.
items.hook: Draw a line from the Tees to the Exe: hard and high to the north-west, soft and low to the south-east.

items.prompt: Dartmoor’s tors are made of which hard igneous rock?
items.explain: Granite formed from magma cooling slowly underground. Weathering along its joints leaves the blocky tors.
items.hook: Granite is grainy: big crystals grew slowly as the magma cooled deep underground.
items.example: Haytor and Hound Tor are two of Dartmoor’s best-known granite tors.

items.prompt: The White Cliffs of Dover and the South Downs are made of which rock?

options.text: Chalk
Granite
options.feedback: Granite is hard and grey, found in places like Dartmoor and the Cairngorms.

options.text: Slate
options.feedback: Slate is in North Wales and the Lake District.

options.text: Basalt
options.feedback: Basalt forms the Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland.

items.explain: Chalk is a soft, white limestone made from the skeletons of tiny sea creatures.
items.hook: Chalk is made of the skeletons of tiny sea plankton: a whole cliff of ancient sea life.
items.example: The Seven Sisters in East Sussex are chalk cliffs; nearby Beachy Head rises about 160 m above the sea.

items.prompt: Clints and grikes (blocks and cracks) at Malham Cove form a limestone pavement. How did the grikes form?

options.text: Acid rainwater dissolved the joints
Earthquakes cracked the rock apart
options.feedback: Weathering, not earthquakes.

options.text: Farmers dug them as drains
options.feedback: They are natural.

options.text: Lava cooled and shrank into blocks
options.feedback: Limestone is sedimentary, not volcanic.

items.explain: This dissolving is called carbonation, a kind of chemical weathering.
items.hook: Grikes are the Gaps; clints are the blocks between them.
items.example: Malham Cove is a curved limestone cliff about 80 m high, with a limestone pavement along its top.

items.prompt: What is the highest mountain in the UK?
items.explain: Ben Nevis is 1,345 m high, in the Scottish Highlands near Fort William.
items.hook: Ben Nevis is 1,345 m: the digits 1-3-4-5, almost counting up.
items.example: The National Three Peaks Challenge climbs Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa).

items.prompt: What is the largest lake in the UK by area?
items.explain: Lough Neagh in Northern Ireland covers about 390 km². Loch Ness holds more water because it is so deep.
items.hook: Lough Neagh wins on area; Loch Ness wins on volume.
items.example: Loch Ness holds more water than all the lakes in England and Wales put together.

items.prompt: Which was the UK’s first national park, created in 1951?
items.explain: The Peak District, between Manchester and Sheffield, is within an hour of millions of people.
items.hook: The Peak was at the peak of the list: the first national park, in 1951.
items.example: The 1932 mass trespass on Kinder Scout helped win the right to roam that led to national parks.

items.prompt: Freeze–thaw weathering is common on British mountains. How does it work?

options.text: Ice expands in cracks
The Sun melts the rock surface
options.feedback: Rock does not melt in sunshine.

options.text: Plant roots dissolve the rock
options.feedback: Roots can widen cracks, but that is biological weathering.

options.text: Waves crash against it
options.feedback: That is erosion at the coast.

items.explain: Water expands by about 9% when it freezes. The broken rock collects as scree below.
items.hook: Water grows by about 9% when it freezes: ice is a wedge that splits rock apart.
items.example: The Wastwater Screes in the Lake District are huge slopes of rock broken off by freeze–thaw.

items.prompt: Explain how rock type affects the landscape of the UK. Use two contrasting examples.
hints: A point linking rock hardness to relief
A first example (e.g. granite on Dartmoor: tors, moorland)
A second, contrasting example (e.g. chalk downs or limestone at Malham)
Mention of weathering or erosion processes
Link to the upland–lowland divide
items.model: Rock type strongly shapes the UK’s landscape because hard rocks resist erosion and soft rocks wear away. On Dartmoor, hard granite forms high, boggy moorland, and freeze–thaw and other weathering along its joints have left blocky tors standing above the land. In contrast, chalk in south-east England is softer and porous, so it forms gentle rolling hills such as the South Downs, with few streams because rain soaks straight in; where chalk meets the sea, it forms white cliffs like Dover. Overall, older, harder rocks in the north and west make upland Britain, while younger, softer rocks in the south and east make lowland Britain, which is roughly the Tees–Exe line.
items.passage:
Dartmoor: granite (igneous, hard, impermeable): high moorland, bogs, tors.
South Downs and Dover: chalk (sedimentary, soft, porous): rolling hills, dry valleys, white cliffs.
Malham, Yorkshire Dales: Carboniferous limestone: limestone pavement, caves, gorges.
The Tees–Exe line divides upland from lowland Britain.

items.prompt: Why is arable farming (growing crops) common in East Anglia?

options.text: Flat, fertile land and dry summers
Its mountains shelter the crops
options.feedback: East Anglia is one of the flattest parts of the UK.

options.text: It rains almost every day
options.feedback: It is one of the driest parts of the UK.

options.text: Sheep cannot survive on its grass
options.feedback: Sheep could, but crops make better use of the land.

items.explain: Wheat, barley and sugar beet are major crops there.
items.hook: East is for eating crops: flat, dry and sunny, perfect for combine harvesters.
items.example: The Fens of Cambridgeshire and Lincolnshire have some of the richest farmland in England.

items.prompt: Why is pastoral farming (raising animals) common in Wales and the Lake District?

options.text: Wet, steep land suits grass
The land is too flat for crops
options.feedback: It is hilly.

options.text: It is too dry for most crops
options.feedback: It is wet, not dry: grass grows well.

options.text: Its soils are the richest in Britain
options.feedback: Machinery struggles on steep, wet land.

items.explain: Hill sheep farming is typical of the uplands.
items.hook: Wet and steep makes grass grow and tractors slip: perfect for sheep.
items.example: Hardy Herdwick sheep graze the Lake District fells.

items.prompt: Farming that uses lots of money, machinery, fertiliser or labour on a small area to get high yields is called…
items.explain: Extensive farming uses large areas with low inputs, like hill sheep farming.
items.hook: Intensive = intense effort on a little land; extensive = extends over a lot of land.
items.example: Heated glasshouses growing tomatoes are very intensive; hill sheep farms are extensive.

items.prompt: Farming to feed your own family, with little or nothing left to sell, is called…
items.explain: Commercial farming produces food to sell for profit.
items.hook: Subsistence: just enough to subsist (survive), with nothing left over to sell.

items.prompt: What is humus?

options.text: Rotted plant and animal matter
A type of soft volcanic rock
options.feedback: It is organic matter, not rock.

options.text: The layer of rock under the soil
options.feedback: That is bedrock.

options.text: A chemical fertiliser for farms
options.feedback: It forms naturally.

items.explain: Humus holds water and nutrients. (The dip is spelled hummus.)
items.hook: Humus is nature’s compost; hummus is a dip. One extra m, a very different meal.

items.prompt: Which practice best protects soil from being washed or blown away?

options.text: Ploughing along the contours
Ploughing straight up and down slopes
options.feedback: Furrows down a slope channel rainwater and soil downhill.

options.text: Removing hedges to make big fields

items.prompt: Explain how physical factors affect the type of farming in different parts of the UK.
hints: Physical factors: climate (rainfall, temperature), relief, soil
An arable example and why it suits the area

items.model: Physical factors largely decide whether land is used for crops or animals. In East Anglia the land is flat, the soils are fertile and summers are warm and fairly dry, so arable farming of wheat, barley and sugar beet is common and large machines work easily. In upland areas such as Wales and the Lake District, rainfall is high, slopes are steep and soils are thin and acidic, so crops struggle; grass grows well, though, so pastoral farming of sheep and cattle dominates. In between, many lowland farms in the wetter west keep dairy cattle on rich grass. Human factors matter too, such as nearness to markets and subsidies, but climate, relief and soil set the basic pattern.
items.passage:
East Anglia: flat; fertile soils; about 600 mm of rain a year; warm summers. Main farming: cereals and sugar beet.
Wales and the Lake District uplands: steep slopes; over 1,500 mm of rain a year in places; thin, acidic soils. Main farming: sheep, some cattle.

items.prompt: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of building large dams to improve water supply.
hints: Advantages: reliable water, irrigation, hydroelectricity, flood control
Disadvantages: people displaced, ecosystems, silt, tension with downstream countries
At least one named example (e.g. Atatürk Dam, Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Three Gorges)
A judgement: do the benefits outweigh the costs?
items.model: Large dams can transform water supply. Their reservoirs store water for dry seasons, supply cities, irrigate farmland and can generate hydroelectric power, as the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile is designed to do for Ethiopia. They can also control floods downstream. However, they have serious costs. Building a reservoir floods land, forcing people from their homes and destroying habitats, and the dam traps silt that used to fertilise farmland downstream. They can also cause tension between countries: Egypt fears the Ethiopian dam will reduce the Nile’s flow, and Syria and Iraq worry about Turkey’s dams on the Euphrates. On balance, large dams can bring major benefits, but only if the costs to people, ecosystems and neighbouring countries are shared fairly and planned for.
items.passage:
Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Blue Nile, Ethiopia: one of Africa’s largest hydroelectric dams; Egypt depends on the Nile for almost all its fresh water.
Atatürk Dam, Euphrates, Turkey: irrigation and power; Syria and Iraq downstream.
Three Gorges Dam, Yangtze, China: more than a million people relocated.

items.prompt: To what extent is tourism good for a popular destination? Use a named example such as Greece, Venice or Kenya.
hints: Economic benefits: jobs, income, the multiplier effect
Problems: overcrowding, pollution, leakage, seasonal jobs, rising house prices
A named example with specific details
How the problems can be managed (e.g. caps, fees, ecotourism)
A judgement that answers “to what extent”
items.model: Tourism brings large benefits to places like Greece. It creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and transport, earns foreign money, and through the multiplier effect wages are spent again in local shops. It also pays to protect historic sites such as the Acropolis. However, too many visitors can damage the very things they come to see. Popular islands face water shortages in summer, crowded streets and rubbish, and many jobs are seasonal and low-paid. When hotels and cruise lines are foreign-owned, some of the profit leaks out of the country. Places are now managing this: Athens uses timed tickets at the Acropolis and Venice has trialled a fee for day visitors. Overall, tourism is good for a destination to a large extent, but only if numbers are managed so that local people and the environment share the benefits.
items.passage: Greece: tens of millions of international visitors a year; tourism is one of the largest parts of the economy. Many jobs are seasonal. Popular islands face summer water shortages. The Acropolis now uses timed tickets to limit crowds. Venice has trialled an entry fee for day visitors.

items.prompt: Explain the causes of desertification in the Sahel, and how people are trying to reduce it.
hints: A definition of desertification
At least two human causes (overgrazing, over-cultivation, deforestation)
Physical causes (drought, climate change)

items.model: Desertification is when land in dry areas becomes desert-like and loses its ability to grow plants. In the Sahel, a growing population has put pressure on the land: overgrazing by large herds strips vegetation, over-cultivation exhausts the soil, and trees are cut down for fuelwood, so bare soil is blown or washed away. Natural droughts, made worse by climate change, add to the problem. People are fighting back. The Great Green Wall, launched in 2007, aims to restore a belt of land across Africa by planting trees and improving farming. On a smaller scale, farmers build low stone lines along slopes to trap rainwater and soil, and protect young trees growing from old roots. Progress is uneven, but these methods show that desertification can be slowed when local people are involved.
items.passage: The Sahel: a semi-arid belt south of the Sahara, about 200–600 mm of rain a year, falling unreliably. Rapidly growing population. Many families depend on herding and farming, and on wood for cooking. The Great Green Wall began in 2007.

items.prompt: Explain why changes in the polar regions matter to people living far away from them.
hints: Sea-level rise from melting land ice
Feedback loops and faster warming (albedo)
Effects on weather, wildlife or shipping

items.model: Changes in the polar regions affect the whole planet. When ice on land in Antarctica and Greenland melts, it adds water to the oceans and raises sea levels, which threatens low-lying cities and countries such as Bangladesh. As Arctic sea ice shrinks, darker ocean water absorbs more sunlight than white ice reflects, so warming speeds up in a positive feedback loop that affects the global climate. Some scientists think a warmer Arctic may also change the paths of weather systems that reach Europe. There are economic effects too, as new shipping routes and resources open up in the Arctic, which could cause tension between countries. So what happens at the poles does not stay at the poles.
items.passage: Antarctica holds about 90% of the world’s ice. If its ice and Greenland’s melted, sea levels would rise by tens of metres (over centuries). Arctic summer sea ice has shrunk sharply since satellite records began in 1979. White ice reflects most sunlight; dark ocean absorbs most of it.

items.prompt: Explain two threats to the world’s oceans and suggest how each could be reduced.
hints: A first threat explained (e.g. plastic pollution)
A realistic way to reduce it
A second threat explained (e.g. overfishing, warming, acidification)
A realistic way to reduce it
items.model: One major threat is plastic pollution. Plastic washes off land and from ships, and ocean currents collect it in gyres such as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch; it breaks into microplastics that animals eat. This could be reduced by cutting single-use plastics, charging for bags and bottles with deposit return schemes, and improving rubbish collection in coastal cities. A second threat is overfishing. When fish are caught faster than they breed, stocks collapse, as cod did on the Grand Banks in 1992. Strict catch quotas, marine protected areas where fishing is banned, and choosing sustainably caught fish can allow stocks to recover.

Cultural variety (languages, religions)
A conclusion
items.model: Describing Africa as one place is misleading because it is a vast and varied continent of 54 countries. Physically it ranges from the Sahara, the largest hot desert, to the rainforests of the Congo basin and the snow-capped volcano of Kilimanjaro. Economies vary too: some countries remain very poor, but others are growing fast, and Kenya’s M-Pesa mobile money service, launched in 2007, was a world first. Culturally there are well over a thousand languages and many religions. Lagos and Johannesburg are huge modern cities, while millions still farm the land. Treating Africa as one place hides this variety and repeats stereotypes about poverty and conflict that do not fit most people’s lives.

items.model: Oil has helped Nigeria’s development in some ways. It brings in most of the country’s export earnings and a large share of government income, which has paid for roads, schools and the new capital, Abuja, and it has created jobs and attracted foreign investment. Relying on one export makes the economy vulnerable when world oil prices fall, and oil wealth has been linked to corruption and inequality. Nigeria is now diversifying into services, telecommunications, farming and film, through Nollywood. Overall, oil has helped Nigeria develop to some extent, but it has not shared its wealth fairly, and other industries will be needed for lasting development.

items.model: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River in China is one of the largest power stations in the world. Its main advantage is clean hydroelectric power, which reduces China’s reliance on coal and cuts air pollution. It also helps control the floods that have killed many thousands of people along the Yangtze, and the reservoir lets large ships travel further inland. However, the costs were huge. More than a million people were moved from their homes, and towns, farmland and archaeological sites were flooded. The dam traps silt, so less reaches the farmland and delta downstream, and the reservoir has been linked to landslides and harm to river wildlife. On balance, the dam has brought major national benefits, but they came at a heavy cost to the people and ecosystems of the valley.
items.passage: Three Gorges Dam, Yangtze River, completed in the 2000s: one of the world’s largest power stations. Reservoir about 600 km long. items.prompt: Explain how India’s physical geography affects the lives of people who live there.

items.model: India’s physical geography shapes daily life. The monsoon brings most of the year’s rain between about June and September, and hundreds of millions of farmers depend on it: a weak monsoon can mean poor harvests and higher food prices, while a very strong one can cause floods. The great rivers, especially the Ganges, flowing from the Himalayas, provide water for farming and cities and are sacred to Hindus, though they can also flood. The Himalayas themselves are a source of water from melting snow and glaciers, a barrier to the north, and a hazard area for earthquakes and landslides. In the north-east, relief rainfall makes places like Mawsynram among the wettest on Earth.

items.prompt: “Protecting the Amazon is the responsibility of the whole world, not just Brazil.” How far do you agree?

items.model: I largely agree, because the Amazon matters to everyone. It stores enormous amounts of carbon, so clearing and burning it speeds up climate change worldwide; it recycles rainfall that farms far beyond the forest depend on; and it holds a huge share of the world’s species. However, it is mostly Brazilian territory, and Brazil has the right to make its own decisions and to develop. Farming, mining and roads bring jobs and income, and many Brazilians are poor. So responsibility should be shared. Richer countries can fund protection, for example by paying to keep forests standing, and consumers and companies can refuse beef and soya grown on newly cleared land. Brazil, in turn, can enforce its laws and protect indigenous territories. The world should share the cost, but Brazil must lead.

items.model: Borders control how people, goods and money move, so they shape everyday life. The border in Ireland shows how sensitive borders can be: an open border helped support peace after the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, so finding a way to avoid checkpoints was a major issue in the Brexit talks.

From 1981 a development corporation attracted investment: offices at Canary Wharf, the Docklands Light Railway, City Airport and thousands of new homes. items.model: I would draw a transect from the town centre outwards and use systematic sampling, stopping every 200 metres. At each site I would complete an environmental quality survey, scoring things like litter, noise, traffic and green space from −2 to +2, and take a photograph. I would also count the number of cars passing in two minutes. For secondary data I would use crime or house-price maps from the internet. I would present the scores on a line graph against distance from the centre and test the pattern with a scatter graph. To make it reliable, two people would score each site and I would repeat it on a second day. I would carry out a risk assessment, for example for busy roads, and work in a group.

items.model: An ecotourism lodge in the rainforest, run with a local community, can be sustainable in all three ways. Environmentally, it uses solar power, collects rainwater and treats its waste, and visitor numbers are limited so the forest and wildlife are protected; some profits fund rangers. Socially, local people are employed as guides and cooks, their culture is respected, and they have a say in decisions. Economically, it earns steady income that stays in the community instead of leaking to foreign companies, which gives people a reason to keep the forest standing rather than sell it for logging. A weakness is that guests still fly long distances, so its carbon footprint is not zero.

A sea wall would protect the town more strongly, but it is very expensive, reflects wave energy that can scour away the beach, and may simply move the problem along the coast. Managed retreat is the most sustainable in the long term, but it would mean many families losing their homes now, which is unfair while cheaper protection is still possible. Rock armour therefore balances cost, fairness and the environment best, while the council plans for retreat in the future.

items.prompt: How well does the Burgess model describe a UK city you know or have studied?
hints: Briefly describe the model
Where the city fits (CBD, inner city, suburbs, fringe)
Where it does not fit (regeneration, out-of-town shopping, social housing on the edge)
A judgement
items.model: The Burgess model shows a city as rings: a central business district, then an inner city of old housing and industry, inner and outer suburbs, and the rural–urban fringe. London fits this broadly. Its CBD in the City and West End has the tallest, most expensive buildings, many inner areas such as Hackney have dense 1800s terraces, and wealthier, lower-density suburbs spread outwards to the green belt. However, it does not fit perfectly. Regeneration has turned former inner-city docks into the skyscrapers of Canary Wharf, some large council estates were built on the edge of the city, and out-of-town retail parks have drawn shops away from the centre. The model is a useful starting point, but real cities are shaped by transport, planning and history as well as distance from the centre.
items.passage:
Burgess model (1920s): rings from the centre: CBD; inner city (factories, 1800s terraces); inner suburbs; outer suburbs; rural–urban fringe.
London examples: the City (CBD); Hackney (Victorian terraces); outer boroughs such as Bromley (suburbs); Canary Wharf (regenerated docks with skyscrapers).

items.prompt: Explain why shared or scarce resources can lead to tension between countries. Use at least one example.
hints: Why scarcity or sharing causes tension (upstream–downstream, competing claims)
A named example (e.g. the Nile, the Euphrates, the Arctic)
How tension could be reduced (treaties, data sharing)
A brief conclusion
items.model: Resources cause tension when they are scarce or when more than one country depends on them. Rivers are a clear example, because the country upstream can control how much water flows downstream. Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile will provide electricity for development, but Egypt, which depends almost entirely on the Nile, fears its water supply will fall. Similarly, as Arctic sea ice melts, countries such as Russia, Canada and Norway are competing to claim newly reachable seabed resources and shipping routes. Tension can be reduced through treaties that share resources fairly, such as the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan, and by sharing data and benefits. Cooperation is possible, but it needs trust and agreed rules.
items.passage:
The Nile: Ethiopia’s Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam is upstream of Sudan and Egypt.
The Arctic: shrinking sea ice is opening routes and seabed resources; Russia, Canada, Norway, Denmark (Greenland) and the USA border it.
Indus Waters Treaty, 1960: shared the rivers of the Indus basin between India and Pakistan for over 60 years; India suspended it in 2025.
